subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
passage:
Jeevan: sachin u there? need a second opinion
Sachin: yeah what happened
Jeevan: Neel hasn't eaten lunch with us for two weeks. Just sits with his bag on his lap
Sachin: maybe he's tired, exams and all
Jeevan: today he said "nothing matters anyway" and laughed like it was a joke. It didn't sound like a joke
Sachin: give him space, it'll pass
Jeevan: I keep telling myself that. But no lunch, going quiet AND saying that. That's three things, not one bad day
Jeevan: if I wait and I'm wrong, he's alone with it. If I ask and I'm wrong, we have one awkward talk
Sachin: ok when you put it like that
Jeevan: tomorrow I sit with him at break and ask him straight. If he shuts me out I tell Ms Fernandes, the counsellor

qa.q: How long has Neel gone without eating lunch with the group?
qa.a: Neel hasn't eaten lunch with them for two weeks.

qa.q: What is Jeevan worried about when he says "if I wait and I'm wrong"?
qa.a: Jeevan is worried that Neel would be left alone with whatever is weighing on Neel, and that uneasy feeling is why Jeevan stops treating it as a passing mood.

qa.q: What alternative approach could work if Neel shuts Jeevan out, and why?
qa.a: Telling Ms Fernandes, the counsellor, as Jeevan plans, could work because a trained adult can help with what a friend cannot carry alone.

qa.q: How might Neel feel if Jeevan sits with him at break and asks straight?
qa.a: Neel might feel relieved that someone noticed, or he might pull away at first, so Jeevan's patience and the counsellor as a back-up both matter.

grounding: A teen weighs three changes in a friend and decides they are serious enough to act on rather than wait out.

subtype: Approach: listening without judging and staying connected [Action]
passage:
Aparna: I'm at the school gate. Come sit with me for ten minutes?
Dhanya: I'm fine, really
Aparna: Okay. I'm still here. No lecture, promise
Dhanya walked out slowly, her bag hanging off one shoulder, and they sat on the low wall by the bicycle stand, Aparna moving her own bag to make room.
Dhanya: everything at home is loud and I feel like I'm disappearing
Aparna: That sounds so heavy. How are you actually doing? Not the "fine" answer
Dhanya: tired. really tired
Aparna: I'm glad you told me. You matter to me, a lot. I can't fix it and I'm not a counsellor, but I can sit here, and I'll check on you tomorrow
Dhanya: ok. thanks for being a real friend and not saying cheer up

qa.q: Where did Aparna and Dhanya sit?
qa.a: They sat on the low wall by the bicycle stand.

qa.q: What was Dhanya feeling when she said everything at home is loud?
qa.a: Dhanya felt overwhelmed and invisible, since she says she feels like she is disappearing, and she also says she is really tired.

qa.q: What could Aparna add if Dhanya's tiredness keeps going, and why?
qa.a: Aparna could encourage Dhanya to talk to a school counsellor or another trusted adult, because Aparna herself says she is not a counsellor and can offer company, not treatment.

qa.q: How might Dhanya experience it that Aparna does not say cheer up?
qa.a: Dhanya probably feels heard and less alone, since nobody is trying to talk her out of her feelings.

grounding: A student sits with her friend, listens without lecturing, asks how she really is, says she matters and names her limits.

subtype: Approach: involving a trusted adult even against a request for secrecy [Action]
passage: Yamini's message came in at lunch: she didn't see the point in anything anymore, and Anirban had to swear he would tell nobody. His hands went cold. He had kept every promise he had ever made her, some of them silly. But he kept hearing how flat her words sounded. After the last bell he walked to the counsellor's room instead of the bus stop. Mrs Kulkarni put down her pen and listened without interrupting. She told him that this was not betrayal and he had done the right thing, and said she would speak with Yamini and her parents that same evening. At home Anirban told his father everything too. His father sat beside him, thanked him, and stayed while Anirban typed: "I'm not angry with you. I told people who can help. I'm still your friend."

qa.q: Who did Anirban tell at school?
qa.a: Anirban told the counsellor, Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling as he chose to break the promise?
qa.a: He felt frightened and torn: his hands went cold, but the flat sound of Yamini's words worried him more than the promise.

qa.q: What could Anirban do alongside telling the adults, and why?
qa.a: He could keep checking in as a friend, as his message shows, because it keeps trust alive while adults handle the proper help.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when the counsellor and her parents get involved?
qa.a: Yamini may feel angry or exposed at first, but Anirban's message that he is not angry and is still her friend gives her a reason to believe he acted from care.

grounding: The teen tells the counsellor and his father despite the promise, believing his friend's safety matters more and adults can arrange help.

subtype: Approach: using helplines and emergency services when danger is immediate [Action]
passage: I'm Bhupen, and I live above the stationery shop, so I see most of what happens on our lane. Tuesday evening Vikas came out of the gully with his phone against his ear, walking so fast he nearly hit my cycle. He was saying, "Papa, come now, it's Ashwin, my best friend, he says he doesn't want to be here anymore, he's at his flat." Then he put his father on hold and dialled the emergency number. He gave the flat number and the building name twice, slowly. He did not run off to Ashwin's himself. When his father's scooter turned in, Vikas pointed and they left together. I couldn't tell whether he was frightened or just sure of what to do. His hands were shaking, but his voice was not. Later his father told me Ashwin was safe and his parents were with him.

qa.q: What did Vikas do after he put his father on hold?
qa.a: He dialled the emergency number and gave the flat number and the building name twice, slowly.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vikas was frightened but steady, and how sure can Bhupen be?
qa.a: His hands were shaking but his voice was not, so he seemed scared yet sure of what to do, though Bhupen admits not being able to tell for certain.

qa.q: If Vikas could not reach his father, what else could he do, and why?
qa.a: He could call a mental health helpline or another adult nearby along with the emergency number, because immediate danger needs adults and trained responders, not a teen alone.

qa.q: How might Ashwin see Vikas's quick calls later?
qa.a: Ashwin may feel frightened or embarrassed, yet also cared for, since a friend acted at once and adults reached him.

grounding: A teen calls a family adult and the emergency number at once when a friend is in immediate danger, seen through a bystander's eyes.

subtype: Approach: trying to fix everything alone [Pitfall]
passage: Kamal's head dropped onto his arm twice during the chemistry lesson. His test slip had come back that morning, 38 out of 100, and he had folded it into his geometry box. Under the desk his phone lit up again: Reena, 2:14 a.m. the night before, then 3:40. He had answered every message, telling her things would be okay, and telling his mother he was studying late. Nobody knew how bad Reena's nights were, not even her parents; she had made him promise. Mr Thomas kept him back after the bell. "You're not yourself, Kamal." "I'm fine, sir, just tired." Mr Thomas said the counsellor's room was open to him, and to any friend he was worried about, and Kamal nodded at the floor. In his pocket the phone buzzed again.

qa.q: When did Reena's messages arrive the night before?
qa.a: Reena's messages came at 2:14 a.m. the night before, then 3:40.

qa.q: What might Kamal be worried about as he says "I'm fine, sir"?
qa.a: Kamal is worried and worn out; he fears breaking Reena's promise, so he hides how much he is carrying.

qa.q: What different approach could Kamal try, and why?
qa.a: Kamal could take up Mr Thomas's offer and bring in the counsellor, so Reena gets proper help and Kamal can sleep and share the load.

qa.q: How does the situation look from Reena's side?
qa.a: Reena may take comfort from Kamal's replies at night, yet nothing deeper changes because no adult knows, and she might worry about Kamal too if she learned what it costs him.

grounding: The student becomes his friend's only support and hides how bad things are, until sleep and marks suffer and the friend still has no professional help.

subtype: Approach: dismissing it as attention seeking [Pitfall]
passage:
“I don't think anyone would even notice if I stopped coming,” Lalremsiami said, eyes on the cracked tiles of the bus stop.
“Oh come on, you say this every exam week.”
“No, I mean it this time. I can't sleep and I don't want to eat.”
“You're exaggerating, Lali. Seriously. Did you finish the maths sheet?”
“Uma, I—”
“The bus is so late. Did you see what Nisha posted?”
Uma told herself it was only a bid for attention from her friend, and that if it were real, Lalremsiami would have said it differently. Lalremsiami looked at her, nodded slowly and pulled her scarf higher. The counsellor's room was two floors above them, and neither mentioned it. On the bus they sat side by side without a word, and Lalremsiami got off two stops early.

qa.q: Where were Uma and Lalremsiami when they talked?
qa.a: They were at the bus stop, and the counsellor's room was two floors above them.

qa.q: What was Uma thinking when she changed the subject?
qa.a: Uma thought it was only a bid for attention, and she probably felt uncomfortable, so she turned to the maths sheet and the late bus.

qa.q: What could Uma try instead, and why?
qa.a: Uma could ask what Lalremsiami means, listen, and offer to walk with her to the counsellor upstairs, because not sleeping, not eating and saying nobody would notice deserve to be taken seriously.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami likely feel after the talk?
qa.a: More alone: she pulled her scarf higher, stayed silent on the bus and got off two stops early.

grounding: A teen tells herself her friend is exaggerating and changes the subject, missing the chance to link her with help.

subtype: Approach: keeping the secret to protect the friendship [Pitfall]
passage: Week three of keeping his friend Rukmini's secret, Sunil could recite her moods like a timetable: quiet before tests, crying behind the library shelves on Thursdays, "I'm fine" whenever anyone walked past. She had said that if he told anyone she would never speak to him again, and he believed her. So in the dining hall he laughed with the others, carried her tray when she couldn't, and lay awake in his hostel bed, afraid of what a silent phone might mean. His hands shook over his chapters. Mr Dutta, the hostel warden, stopped by his table. "Everything all right, Sunil? You look worn out." Sunil's mouth opened. "Yes, sir. Just exams." Mr Dutta nodded slowly and said his door stayed open. Across the hall Rukmini's seat was empty again, and nobody who could help knew why.

qa.q: Who asked Sunil if everything was all right?
qa.a: Mr Dutta, the hostel warden, asked Sunil that.

qa.q: What was Sunil afraid of when he kept quiet?
qa.a: Sunil feared that Rukmini would never speak to him again, and he was also afraid of what a silent phone might mean.

qa.q: What different approach could work here, and why?
qa.a: Sunil could go to Mr Dutta, whose door stays open, so trained adults can support Rukmini and Sunil no longer carries it alone.

qa.q: How might Mr Dutta see Sunil's answer?
qa.a: Mr Dutta sees a worn-out student and cannot know why, so he offers his open door, but without more information he cannot help Rukmini.

grounding: A student keeps a friend's distress secret for weeks to protect the friendship, carrying too much and delaying care.

subtype: Approach: caring for own limits and feelings [Revision]
passage: Come sit, beta. Your Aditi Masi has a story. When I was sixteen, my friend Sonali went through a very dark stretch, and I was the one she called, sometimes three times a night. I never said no. Then one morning I was crying into my cereal for no reason, and my hands wouldn't stop trembling before a test. I realised I had nothing left. That evening I told Amma all of it. She didn't scold me. She hugged me, and the next day we phoned Sonali's mother together and spoke to the school counsellor. I stayed her friend, sat beside her at lunch and slipped silly notes into her bag. But I stopped being her only rope. That was the kindest thing I did, for both of us.

qa.q: Who did Aditi tell that evening?
qa.a: Aditi told Amma that evening, all of it.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling before she spoke to Amma?
qa.a: Aditi was exhausted and anxious: she cried into her cereal for no reason, her hands trembled before a test and she had nothing left.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling Amma was the turning point, because it brought in Sonali's mother and the counsellor, so Aditi could stay a friend without being Sonali's only support.

qa.q: How might Sonali have experienced Aditi sharing the support with adults?
qa.a: Sonali may have felt worried or exposed at first, yet she gained more people who could help, while Aditi still sat beside her at lunch and slipped notes into her bag.

grounding: After heavy conversations a teen notices her exhaustion and anxiety, tells her mother, shares the support with adults and keeps a friendly role.

subtype: Approach: following up after the first conversation [Revision]
passage: Okay, first, I'm Santosh, and I'm no expert. Amma calls me her boy, and this is the boy's story. My friend Gargi told me on a Monday that she felt like a burden, and I said the right things, I think. But my mother says one talk is only the start, so on Tuesday I texted her, "Hey, how's today?" She wrote "okay." The next week I asked her to walk round the lake with me after school. She talked for a bit, then went quiet, and I could see she was still barely eating, still not smiling with her eyes. That's when I understood that checking in alone wasn't enough. I told her I was worried and asked if we could tell her parents together. She cried, but she said yes. Her mother hugged us both. It isn't fixed. But more people are holding it now.

qa.q: Where did Santosh invite Gargi to walk?
qa.a: He asked her to walk round the lake with him after school.

qa.q: Why did Santosh ask Gargi about telling her parents?
qa.a: He was worried because she was still barely eating and not smiling with her eyes, and he understood that checking in alone wasn't enough.

qa.q: What could Santosh add if Gargi's family cannot fully help, and why?
qa.a: He could bring in a school counsellor or another trusted adult, since more trained people can arrange proper help than a friend can.

qa.q: How might Gargi's mother have felt when she was told?
qa.a: She was probably worried and shaken, but also grateful that Gargi and Santosh came to her, since she hugged them both and could now help.

grounding: A teen checks in the next day and the next week, invites his friend for a walk and involves her family when she still struggles.

passage: Amara wrote it on the back of her maths notebook during study hall, words for her friend Selin. Start small: "Lately you seem really down, and I'm worried about you. Can I sit with you?" She whispered it to the bus window, then again to the mirror at home. What if Selin gets angry? Then: "Okay, no pressure. I'm still here." What if Selin goes silent and stares at the floor? Then wait, don't fill the quiet, and say, "We don't have to talk right now." What if nothing works? Then tell Mrs Okafor, the school nurse, tomorrow. She read the list twice, folded it into her pocket and found Selin by the lockers, heart thudding, hoping the words would come out the way they sounded at home.

qa.q: Where did Amara write her plan?
qa.a: Amara wrote it on the back of her maths notebook during study hall.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling as she went to find Selin?
qa.a: Amara was nervous: her heart was thudding and she hoped the words would come out the way they sounded at home.

qa.q: What other step could Amara add if Selin shuts down, and why?
qa.a: She could do as her list says, leave the quiet and say they don't have to talk now, then tell Mrs Okafor, because a trusted adult can offer help she cannot.

qa.q: How might Selin experience being approached by the lockers?
qa.a: Selin might feel surprised, exposed or relieved that someone noticed, and calm words like no pressure leave room to answer.

grounding: A student plans simple words and responses for an angry or silent friend before approaching a struggling friend.
